title: Benchmark methodology workshop - runtime/VPC/KV-cache/batching/quant (deep dive)
summary: Deep-dive on benchmark methodology to compare runtime performance across hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) setups. Covered apples-to-apples prompt sets, load generation, and how KV cache, batching, and quantization affect tail latency and throughput. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share harness, synthetic load scripts, baseline configs, and schedule pilot benchmark with Northbridge infra team.
transcript:
00:00 Aisha Khan: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, we planned a 90 minute deep dive today on benchmark methodology, please mute when not speaking.
00:12 Dana Li: Thanks Aisha, excited — we've been asked to validate performance across our private VPC and a potential dedicated offering.
00:22 Ben Park: Great, we'll go through the prompt sets, load generation, and how KV cache and batching affect tail latency and throughput. Note: some auto-transcription quirks may show up.
00:35 Mark Reynolds: Quick context — we run a mix of short chat queries and longer completion tasks, median len around 120 tokens but heavy tail to 1024 in some workflows. Our current infra is k8s on GCP with private subnets.
00:50 Emily Zhao: Thanks, that helps. Two initial questions — what's your SLO for p50/p95 latency and what cost envelopes should we aim for?
01:05 Priya Singh: We need p95 under 600ms for short chat paths, and p99 ideally under 1.5s. Cost is TBD but we want to evaluate cost/latency tradeoffs.
01:18 Ben Park: Good, that sets targets. For apples-to-apples we recommend identical prompt sets, same model checkpoints, same tokenization configs, and matching sequence length caps. We'll also control for batch sizes and KV cache enabled/disabled.
01:33 Dana Li: On prompt sets — we have sensitive PHI-ish content; can we anonymize?
01:40 Aisha Khan: Absolutely, we provide a prompt scrubber script or you can share sanitized examples. The benchmark harness supports redaction.
01:48 Ben Park: For load generation, we recommend a two-phase approach: ramp + steady state then spike tests. Use real inter-arrival distributions — not just flat RPS. We'll share our locust/JMeter scripts but we can also run from your VPC for on-prem tests.
02:05 Mark Reynolds: Important to ensure the KV cache warmup is accounted for. How long should we run warmup?
02:12 Ben Park: Warmup depends on working set. For chat-like workloads we typically do 15-30 minutes of representative traffic to populate prefix cache; measure cold vs warm startup separately.
02:25 Dana Li: Can you clarify how you measure per-token cost when batching? We saw numbers that looked optimistic because they averaged over merged tokens.
02:35 Emily Zhao: Good point — we report both aggregate per-token and per-request cost. For batching you must show effective tokens-per-second and also amortized latency per request. We'll include batch histograms.
02:48 Priya Singh: Quantization — we use int8 for cost savings. How do you handle quality regressions?
02:55 Ben Park: We run eval prompt sets and embedding similarity/regression checks. For quantization we surface BLEU/ROUGE/embedding cosine delta and have rollback thresholds. It's important to run the same evals on float32 and quantized variants.
03:12 Mark Reynolds: VPC/on-prem differences — network overheads and NLB TLS termination could add jitter. Any recommended measurement controls?
03:22 Aisha Khan: For on-prem we recommend colocating load generators in same network zone or using a mirrored replay to avoid internet variance. Capture network metrics separately and annotate traces.
03:35 Oliver Grant: Are there tools to do apples-to-apples across hardware? It's hard when GPUs differ — A100 vs H100 vs smaller cards.
03:44 Ben Park: We normalize by measured token compute (tokens/sec/GPU) and also include target hardware description in the report. Where possible we run same model binary compiled with identical kernels. When that's impossible we report config differences and show cost-normalized curves.
04:03 Dana Li: We care about tail latency for interactive apps — can your harness measure p99.9?
04:10 Ben Park: Yes, we collect microsecond-resolution timestamps and will surface p50/p95/p99/p99.9. For p99.9 we recommend long-duration runs or synthetic heavy tails.
04:23 Mark Reynolds: What's your recommended method for KV cache experiments?
04:28 Emily Zhao: Run three buckets — cold (no cache), warm (steady working set), and degraded (simulate evictions). Capture hit rates, miss patterns, and the effect on decode latency. Also test varying prefix reuse rates — e.g., 10%, 30%, 60% reuse.
04:48 Priya Singh: Do we need to disable batching in some runs to isolate KV effects?
04:52 Ben Park: Yes, isolate variables — do single-factor experiments: batching only, cache only, quant only, then combined. Interactions can be nonlinear.
05:05 Dana Li: Regarding quantization, how do we ensure the same seed/initialization across runs?
05:12 Ben Park: Use the same model checkpoint and fixed rng seeds where possible, and snapshot model binaries. We'll document the binary and kernel versions.
05:24 Mark Reynolds: Security — we need audit logs, keys in KMS, and SOC2 artifacts. Can dedicated or private deployments integrate with our KMS/HSM?
05:33 Aisha Khan: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem HSM. We'll share security whitepaper and SOC2 report. We'll also demonstrate audit log exports during the pilot.
05:48 Oliver Grant: One gotcha we saw — different tokenizers across runtimes causing subtle token count differences which skew per-token cost.
05:55 Emily Zhao: We'll verify tokenizer versions and run token counting cross-checks. The harness includes a tokenizer checker.
06:07 Priya Singh: For apples-to-apples, do you recommend locking model optimization flags (like fused kernels) even if they differ per-hardware?
06:16 Ben Park: Lock what you can. If kernel selection differs, document it and include a sensitivity analysis. Also run a reference baseline with generic kernels for fairness.
06:30 Mark Reynolds: Practical question — what's a minimal benchmark plan we can run within 2 weeks?
06:36 Aisha Khan: Minimal plan: 1) share sanitized prompt set and workload profile, 2) Redwood provides harness and baseline configs, 3) run a 2-hour warmup+1-hour steady state on your VPC and a hosted dedicated stage, 4) exchange logs and we run analysis.
06:51 Dana Li: That timeline works. Any prerequisites on our side?
06:55 Emily Zhao: Access for load generator or ability to run our container, sanitized data, and a point contact for network/firewall rules.
07:05 Ben Park: We'll also provide an instrumentation checklist: metrics exporters, tracing hooks, and a small script to validate tokenization parity.
07:18 Priya Singh: Who owns the baseline config?
07:21 Aisha Khan: Redwood will propose a baseline; you can tweak. We'll version configs in the repo we share.
07:30 Mark Reynolds: Competitors — we may compare to Vertex and our own in-house endpoints. Expect some questions on how you measured their numbers.
07:39 Ben Park: We'll capture configuration notes for competitor setups and avoid black-box assumptions.
07:46 Dana Li: Anything else on evaluation metrics?
07:49 Emily Zhao: Include user-perceived latency, decode time, kernel time, GPU utilization, cost per 1M tokens, and quality regressions. Also include per-route breakdowns.
08:05 Aisha Khan: Recap: Redwood shares harness, anonymized prompt scrubber, locust scripts, baseline configs, and security docs. Northbridge runs minimal plan within 2 weeks. Schedule follow-up to review results.
08:18 Mark Reynolds: Sounds good.
08:22 Dana Li: Quick side note — can you run a micro-benchmark for 1:1 latency on our smallest model to prove tail behavior?
08:29 Ben Park: Yes, we can run that as part of the pilot.
08:33 Priya Singh: Thanks all.
08:35 Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone, we'll send the repo and action items after the call.
08:40 [call ends with briefly overlapping chatter and a link posted to the meeting chat: /bench-harness repo link]
